_comment: Canonical-form conformance vectors for Agoreum signed documents.
Settlement receipts and reputation attestations both, because they are
the same object: one key, one canonical form, one key document,
differing only in which field carries the payload. A realistic vector
for each is what stops that claim being true only in the code that
asserts it.
Every implementation of the published verification rule must turn each
`value` below into exactly the `canonical` string. There are four:
the API that signs (Python), the browser verifier (TypeScript), and the
Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs.
This file exists because the rule has now been under-specified three
times, and every one was found by writing another implementation rather
than by reading the sentence again:
1. Escaping. Python escaped non-ASCII to \uXXXX by default and
JavaScript never has, so any accented character diverged.
2. Collation. `keys sorted` did not say sorted by what. JavaScript
compares UTF-16 code units, Python and Go order by code point, and
they disagree above U+FFFF.
3. Numbers. Python writes 1.0 where JavaScript and Go write 1, Python
writes 1e-07 where they write 1e-7, and integers past 2^53 lose
precision in a parser backed by doubles.
Each of those was unreachable when found: no receipt carried an accent,
a data-derived key, or a float. That is the point. They would have
surfaced as a genuine receipt whose signature did not verify, and the
reasonable reaction to that is to stop checking signatures.
`canonical` is the exact string that gets UTF-8 encoded and signed. It is
written here as a literal rather than computed by any implementation, so
that all four are pinned to the same constant instead of agreeing with
each other and with nothing else.
`rejected` cases must be refused rather than canonicalised, because their
canonical form is not the same in every language.
`detectable_by` says which implementations can actually assert a case, and
the reason is worth understanding rather than working around. JSON does
not distinguish 1.0 from 1, so by the time a value has been through a
parser the evidence may be gone:
- `{"a":1.0}` reaches Python as a float and JavaScript as the integer
1. Only Python can see it, and only Python needs to: JavaScript would
write `1`, which is what a correct signer would have signed anyway.
- `{"a":0.1}` is a non-integer everywhere, so every implementation can
refuse it.
parser rounded it before any check could run, so a verifier cannot
detect it at all.
That last one is the architectural point: **the safe-integer rule can only
be enforced where the receipt is created.** A verifier is handed a value
whose corruption already happened. So the signer refuses, and the
verifiers assert what they can still see.

accepted.name: keys are sorted, not left in insertion order
sorting reaches every level, not only the top
arrays keep their order, unlike object keys
control characters are still escaped, as JSON requires
keys sort by code point, not by UTF-16 code unit
the largest integer that survives a double
a realistic reputation attestation

_comment: x402 receipt conformance. An x402 receipt is a JWS Compact
Serialization signed by Agoreum and verified against the DID document
at did:web:agoreum.xyz, which is a different check from the native
receipt above: JWS carries its own encoded payload, so the signing
input is the two segments joined by a dot as ASCII, and canonical JSON
does not enter into it.
That difference is the reason these vectors exist. An implementer who
reuses the canonical form here writes a verifier that rejects every
genuine receipt whose producer serialised the payload even slightly
differently, and the visible symptom is a real receipt looking forged.
**Each fixture is stored as `segments`, to be joined with a dot.** Not
a style choice and not to be tidied back into one string. Whole JWSs
here made gitleaks' `jwt` rule fire twenty-six times, once per fixture
per copy of this file, every one a false positive. The alternatives
were a path allowlist, which would switch the scanner off across a
file that also carries private key seeds, or thirteen exact-value
exceptions that would go stale the next time these are regenerated.
Storing segments needs no exception at all, so the secret scan keeps
its complete ruleset over this file. One segment joins to itself and
two join to an unsigned JWS, which is how the two malformed cases are
expressed without special handling.
The keys below are derived from the seed bytes 0..31 and 32..63 and are
published on purpose. Every signature in this file can be regenerated
from them, which is what makes these fixtures checkable rather than
opaque. Neither is, or may ever be, a key that signs anything real.
Every rejected case names an `expect_reason` its refusal must contain.
That is not decoration. The first version of this block asserted only
that a case was refused, and three of its cases were refused by the
signature check rather than by the check they were named after: the
header is inside the signing input, so editing `alg` or adding `crit`
and keeping the original signature breaks the signature. Deleting the
algorithm and extension checks outright left every suite green. The
header variants are genuinely signed now, and a refusal that names the
wrong reason fails.
The last five cases carry real signatures and are about authority
rather than cryptography. They are the ones a verifier passes by
accident.

did_web_urls.why: the plain case, and the one Agoreum actually publishes
colons after the host are path segments, and there is no .well-known
a port is percent-encoded, so splitting on ':' without decoding gives the wrong host

accepted.name: a genuine receipt naming no transaction
accepted.why: the signature is valid and it still proves no settlement. The result must distinguish the two rather than report a valid signature and stop

rejected.name: the payload is edited to redirect the payer
rejected.why: the only case here that is genuinely about the signature: the bytes changed under a signature that still claims to cover them

rejected.name: alg is downgraded to none
rejected.why: signed for real, so the signature check passes it and only the header check refuses it. Built with the original signature in the first version, which meant this vector tested the signature check and nothing else

rejected.name: alg claims a symmetric algorithm
rejected.why: a verifier that dispatched on alg would hand an Ed25519 public key to an HMAC as a shared secret. This one never dispatches, and still refuses rather than ignoring the field

rejected.name: an unknown critical header extension
rejected.why: RFC 7515 requires refusal when crit names an extension the verifier does not implement. Genuinely issued and genuinely unreadable: accepting it means reporting a receipt as verified while dropping the condition attached to it

rejected.name: the kid names a key the document does not publish
rejected.why: signed by the right party under a key id nothing resolves, which is what a rotation away from a compromised key looks like

rejected.name: no kid at all
rejected.why: a signature attributable to nobody, even though it is a real one

rejected.name: not a compact JWS
rejected.why: refused by shape, so malformed input does not read as forgery. One segment joins to itself

rejected.name: two segments rather than three
rejected.why: an unsigned JWS is not a receipt

rejected.name: the signature is valid but the caller expected another signer
rejected.why: the refusal must name who actually signed. Without that the caller is told the document is wrong rather than that it came from somebody else

rejected.name: a complete forgery, signed by another DID and checked against that DID's own document
rejected.why: the attack the pin exists for, and the only vector that is internally consistent end to end. Everything agrees: the key signs, the document publishes it, assertionMethod authorises it. Nothing but the pinned DID separates it from a genuine receipt

rejected.name: the DID document describes a different subject
rejected.why: the document is not the one that should have been fetched, whatever it contains

rejected.name: the key is published but not under assertionMethod
rejected.why: a key in the document is not thereby authorised to make claims

rejected.name: the key is authorised for authentication but not assertion
rejected.why: the distinction Agoreum's own document draws deliberately. A verifier that ignores the relationship discards it
